title: Neuroscience
intro: The biology that spiking models are trying to capture: how the neocortex is built, how neurons and populations behave as dynamical systems, how a small insect brain learns, how population activity hides low-dimensional structure, and which kinds of neuron the brain is made of.

blocks.text: Spiking neural networks are only as useful as the biology they borrow from. This part of the library collects the neuroscience behind the models: not every detail of the brain, but the circuits and ideas that a builder of a spiking cortical column needs to know. Each page explains the biology, the main theories, and where possible gives you a small simulation to play with.

items: Cortical Columns (#/neuroscience/cortical-columns): the neocortex's repeating six-layer circuit, the idea that it is a generic computing unit, and the theories built on that idea. Its sub-pages cover the Thousand Brains Theory, temporal memory in minicolumns, grid cells and reference frames, and a practical blueprint for building a column from spiking neurons.

Neuronal Dynamics (#/neuroscience/neuronal-dynamics): phase-plane analysis, excitability and bifurcations of single neurons, and population activity, the mathematics of how neurons and groups of neurons behave over time.
Mushroom Bodies (#/neuroscience/mushroom-bodies): the insect learning centre, a clean example of sparse expansion coding and of reward-gated plasticity onto a few output neurons.

Neural Manifolds (#/neuroscience/neural-manifolds): the low-dimensional surfaces that population activity lives on, continuous attractor networks, generalized synchronization and how these relate to theories of cortical inference such as the free energy principle.

Neural Cell Types (#/neuroscience/cell-types): the main kinds of neuron (cortical pyramidal cells and interneurons, hippocampal, cerebellar, thalamic, basal ganglia, sensory and motor neurons) and glia, with the computational models that exist for each, from detailed multi-compartment reconstructions to Izhikevich and integrate-and-fire point models.

blocks.text: If your goal is to understand computational cortical columns, read Cortical Columns first for the anatomy and the big picture, then Temporal Memory (how one layer of a column learns sequences), Grid Cells and Reference Frames (how a column could know where its sensor is), and The Thousand Brains Theory (how many columns together recognise objects). Finish with Building a Column from Spiking Neurons, which turns those ideas into an engineering plan that uses the neuron models (#/snn/neuron-models) and learning rules (#/snn/learning-rules) elsewhere in the library. Neuronal Dynamics and Neural Manifolds are the mathematical background; dip into them when a model's behaviour surprises you. Neural Cell Types is the reference shelf: when you add a population to your column, look up its cell type there for the biology and a published model to start from.

A note on certainty: anatomy such as the six layers and the existence of grid cells is well established. Theories of what columns compute, including the Thousand Brains Theory, are serious, published hypotheses but are not settled science. Pages mark which is which.

Sources: Gerstner, Kistler, Naud & Paninski, Neuronal Dynamics (Cambridge University Press, 2014); Mountcastle, 'The columnar organization of the neocortex', Brain (1997); Hawkins, A Thousand Brains: A New Theory of Intelligence (Basic Books, 2021).
